feat: harden sandbox builds and hold wide slices for approval (#127)
message:
* feat: harden sandbox builds and hold wide slices for approval

Sandbox builds and evaluation:
- Scan public files and starters for credentials (secret_found, file/line/rule,
  never the value) and block slices that include credentials files; one
  isSecretPath shared by core and the agent's repo tools.
- Confine fixtures and walkthroughs (confined.ts + the worker's AST check),
  including quoted destructuring keys, `x! / y`, `new Date(...)` spreads,
  Intl/Temporal.
- Mock packages that a lockfile or npm/Yarn config sends to a non-public
  registry (Yarn Berry reads only .yarnrc.yml); rename mocked packages and env
  reads, refusing Node built-ins and Node/npm-affecting variables.
- Scan organization names by distinctive word; take GitHub noreply logins and
  drop role mailboxes and numeric terms.
- Run each hidden test twice (flaky) and read passes from TAP counts;
  gradingTree for submissions.
- local-process: per-job uid when root, startup probe, quarantine on failed
  sweep, per-job TMPDIR, empty cache for lockfile preparation, hardened reads;
  lockfile store accepts only registry tarballs matching their path. Refused
  with NODE_ENV=production; env files masked in the worker container.

Slicing and pricing:
- Stubs drop comments, private member names and literal values; namespace
  imports narrow to the names they read.
- Slices wider than AUTO_SLICE_LIMITS are measured for pricing but held at
  awaiting_approval; owners/admins approve via POST .../slice/approve before
  anything is prepared or cut (idempotent, refused while published).

Web: a cover while leaving for GitHub/Jira, with Cancel after 10s, Escape,
and the app inert behind it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: close review gaps in sandbox hardening

- Worker: mount the checkout read-only in root's home and copy what the
  worker builds into /repo, so job uids cannot write anything the worker,
  other containers or the host run next (Docker Desktop bind mounts let any
  uid write). The uid sweep must exit cleanly and a /proc scan must confirm
  nothing is left, else the uid is quarantined; it also removes the uid's
  files under /tmp, /var/tmp and /dev/shm. npm logs go to the job's temp
  dir and the per-uid cache keeps only _cacache. EVALUATION_JOB_UID ranges
  that reach 65534/65535 or past 2e9 are refused.
- Vocabulary: workspace and private-registry packages' scopes and
  multi-word names are scanned, so an un-renamed private package blocks
  vocabulary_leaked.
- Secrets: generic rule matches only names ending in a secret word and skips
  paths, ARNs and joined-word values; placeholders exempt provider tokens and
  URL passwords only as the whole value; new SendGrid, Hugging Face, Bearer
  and npm _authToken rules; isSecretPath covers .envrc, *.env, secrets.*,
  tfvars, kubeconfig, .pgpass, .pypirc, .git-credentials, docker config,
  *.p8, *.ppk and more.
- Slice approval: the preparer's hold of a legacy wide profile is a no-op
  once approved (holdSlice); a cut is requested as the recorded approver.
- flow_wait counts awaiting_approval as measured and times the first
  measured transition, not updated_at (migration 0072).
- gradingTree's task-code check is documented as an advisory lint, with a
  few more cheap catches; grading must isolate task code by process.
- Web: cancelling the leaving cover reopens run streams and refetches.
- Tests for each, including real-Postgres tests for approveSlice/holdSlice
  and migration 0071 on populated rows.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: unblock sandbox hardening CI

- isSecretPath matches key JSON on the stem instead of `.*\.json$`, which
  CodeQL flagged as polynomial backtracking on repeated keywords.
- Worker smoke expects the widened stub (`declare const value: number;`),

message:
* feat: make the flows feel faster

Phase 5 of docs/plan/faster-flows.md.

- A push channel per workspace (GET /api/v1/orgs/:orgId/events): the
  stores announce run and profile changes on `run_changed`, the API
  fans them out, and the web app re-reads what changed, slowing its
  polls to 15 s while the stream is open.
- A build uploads its generated project before the baseline
  (analysis_run.preview, migration 0068); the version's files serve it
  as provisional, and the sandbox tab links to it.
- Stages show the workspace's typical wait beside their clock
  (GET .../flows/typical, from flow_wait_sample).
- Fewer waterfalls: a bounty reads with its live proposal, spec and
  profiles (?with=live); /me/orgs answers each workspace's setup; a
  snapshot's runs come with their builders' artifacts.
- LoadingLine shows after 150 ms; the file viewer and diagram renderer
  are lazy chunks.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: close gaps found reviewing the faster flows

Found reviewing phases 0 to 5 of docs/plan/faster-flows.md and testing
them on a development stack. Each fix has a test that fails without it.

- Phase 0: flow_wait_sample counted a run that wrote no proposal as a
  price, measured `run:<tool>` from the run's creation (so it included
  the queue), and took weeks in the session's time zone. A price now ends
  at the proposal written, the rubric counts the same runs as the price,
  `run:` starts at the claim, and weeks are UTC (migration 0069). The
  views are checked against Postgres in flow-wait.integration.ts.
- Phase 1: a slice whose build met the run cap cleared its cut request
  first, so the cut draft was never built. The request now stays for the
  cutter's next pass.
- Phase 2: the mkdtemp roots made each restart start an empty cache and
  leave the old one on disk. The source and npm caches live under the
  worker user's ~/.cache/sandbox-factory instead, which no other user can
  create first.
- Phase 2: a run sharing another's fill failed when that run's deadline
  or lease cut it; it now fills again with its own. An eviction no longer
  removes an entry a run took, or a key refilled, while it was awaiting.
- Phase 4: a failure of the hidden-tests agent started beside the first
  baseline failed builds that needed no hidden tests. It now fails only
  a build whose baseline lacks them, as before the agent ran beside it.
- Phase 4: a run ending while a claim for the other slots was out left
  the loop in its 5 s idle wait (graphify to abstractions: 5.03 s, now
  28 ms). The loop claims again at once.
- Phase 5: a stream the browser gave up on (an HTTP error on reconnect,
  as a deploy gives) stayed closed while views used it. It is opened
  anew, backing off from 5 s to 60 s.
- The sandbox file viewer test waits 5 s for its lazy chunk, as the rest
  of its file does.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: close gaps found testing the faster flows

- Source cache: overlapping evictions recount from live entries instead
  of over-deleting; a run waiting on another's fill honours its own abort
  signal and is no longer reported as a cache hit (its wait is timed as
  fetch).
- Bounty read with ?with=live answers from stored data and never waits on

- Tests: agent-loop result order, upload concurrency, source-cache LRU,

- Core: pricing arithmetic, stage rules, handles, aliases, the slice walk

subject: feat(sandbox): write hidden tests for sliced versions, and hold slicing while published (#98)
message:
* feat(sandbox): write hidden tests for sliced versions, and build slices against the declarations they were checked with

A sliced version's baseline could never pass:

- The build declared every package as an untyped shorthand module under
  the source's strict options, while the slice was checked against a
  module per package exporting each name it reads as a value and a type,
  with noImplicitAny off. A type import from a package (the repository's
  own workspace packages among them) failed the build with TS2709, and a
  callback on an untyped value with TS7006. The build now writes the same
  declarations (packageModules, shared with the slice's shim) and relaxes
  noImplicitAny as the check does.
- A sliced draft starts with no hidden tests, so no submission could be
  judged. When a build's baseline fails for that alone, an agent reads
  the public project and the approved spec, writes hidden tests, and runs
  each candidate set through a fresh baseline (at most 5 runs). A set is
  kept only once its baseline passes; it settles on the draft with the
  build's evidence and the transform it hashes to when the run commits.

The build tool is sandbox_build@5 and is queued with the agent deadline.
Slice again is no longer held for a draft an older builder built, and its
hold says a new price cuts a new slice. The starter's per-run report moved
to sandbox-build.ts (reportedBaselineOf) for both agents to use.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Contributors work in the version a sandbox publishes, so `POST .../slice`

* feat(deepwiki): write concise wikis in parallel from a fresh clone

A wiki took about eight minutes: some twenty pages written one by one.
The local DeepWiki-Open service now writes eight pages at a time, and the
worker asks for a concise wiki of four to six pages.

The service also indexed a repository once and never refreshed its
clone, so every later wiki described the first commit it saw. Patches
mounted into the image fetch the default branch's head before each wiki
and re-embed only the chunks that changed; the token is passed to git
through the environment and no longer left in the clone's remote URL.

* feat(web): animate approving and unapproving a bounty's steps

Approving a step's version used to snap from one look to the other. Now,

- The brand line along the version card's top draws round both sides

The flash, dip, glint and shake play only on a change seen on the page,
never on arrival. A tab's content keeps its tooltip with or without a

goes. All of it is still for those who ask for less motion.

A proposal watched being sized now keeps its streamed parts on screen

* feat(analysis): build a repository's context at one commit

Every context builder is read at one commit: the snapshot the repository's

snapshot no longer changes what the rows show; the block names the context's
commit, says when the chosen one differs, and "Build all" there moves every
builder to it. Runs on other snapshots stay cached, so moving back is free.

The block offers "Build all" and "View all" side by side, and each built row

* feat(bounties): a bounty's work may touch any of the workspace's repositories

A bounty names no repository, and neither does a board: `bounty.repo_id`
and `jira_board.source_repo_id` go (migration 0059). The drafting model is
shown an outline of each of the workspace's repositories under a label and
says which the work changes; the proposal records them as `repositories`,
each at the snapshot it was drafted beside, and a profile is measured in
each (`bounty_profile` is unique per proposal, revision and snapshot). The
backfill makes a proposal's one snapshot the one repository it touches.

`rubric-v2` scores the code over every repository the work touches: counts
summed, modules named by repository and charged beyond each repository's
first, and four points per repository beyond the first for the integration
across them. The code is all of them or none: when a touched snapshot is
gone by the time the proposal is written, none is profiled and the code is
unavailable, so the model's size stands rather than a size scored from part
of the work. A profile's settle meets the others' writes, so the rubric is
tried again once per profile, and reports `bounty_rubric_contended` if it
still cannot write.

GitHub context is the workspace's repositories' documents, synced as one
source. A repository its connection cannot read is unread, and counts at
its snapshot, so a sync is never ahead of itself; the ahead warning names
the repository with new commits, or says the set changed. Documents from a
repository no outline holds are headed as another repository, never by an
outline's label.

A sandbox is cut from the one connected repository the sizing touches, and
generated from the bounty when it touches none or several; the page and the
API now count connected repositories with one shared check,
`isWorkspaceSource`. Its stack, and the bounty's inherited stack, are the
touched repositories', or any of the workspace's before sizing names one.

ship.sh notes that an agent running it monitors the PR and resolves what
blocks it until it merges into main.

message:
* feat(pricing): size proposals by a rubric of scenarios, test cases and code

A bounty's size is now scored from countable evidence rather than the
model's judgement alone. The rubric (`packages/core/src/pricing/rubric.ts`,
rubric-v1) sums three dimensions:

- Scenarios: each scenario's weight, plus open questions.
- Test cases: one per scenario, plus each outcome step beyond a test's
  first.
- Code: the complexity profile's slice size, touched modules, services,
  seams, untested modules, migrations, stubs and blockers, less a
  discount for an analogous pattern.

The total falls in a band of the nine priced sizes, which the rate card
prices. Sizing stores the assessment with the code pending, so the model's
size stands; when the profiler settles a profile, the rubric re-scores the
spec and sizes a proposed proposal by it. A reviewer's resize stands and
the rubric is recorded beside it, offered back through
`POST .../proposals/:id/rubric`. A respec of a rubric-sized proposal is
priced at the rubric's score of the changed spec.

The Price tab shows the working: each dimension's factors with their
evidence and points, a ladder of every size's points and price on the
proposal's card, and the rules themselves.

Migration 0051 adds `bounty_proposal.rubric` and lets `sized_by` be
`rubric`.

* feat(sandbox): stack approval and publication, with an expiry date

A sandbox is published only over an approved bounty, and the approval
cannot be taken back (unapprove, with or without Jira, or re-price) while
the sandbox is published. Both sides lock the proposal row before reading
the other, so concurrent publish and unapprove cannot both commit.

Every publication now runs until an expiry date. Publish opens a popup
with quick actions (1, 3 or 7 days) and a calendar; picking one publishes.
A publication past its date reads as expired: it no longer holds the
approval, and the version can be published again. Adds sandbox.expires_at
(migration 0052).

Disabled actions explain themselves in a tooltip. The bounty card shows a
dash for an unapproved bounty's price and size, and a live publication's
pill opens its sandbox.

* feat(github): list a repository's branches and pull one into a snapshot

with the commit it is at, the first 300 (`GET .../repositories/:id/
branches`). An owner or admin pulls one (`POST .../repositories/:id/
snapshots` with `{ branch }`): the default branch is synced as the sweep
syncs it, so the head moves; any other branch's ref is read and that
commit queued under `refs/heads/<branch>`. A commit already snapshotted
answers with its snapshot; otherwise 202 with the commit, and the
snapshot lands in the background.

Each branch waits in its own line in the snapshotter, and only the
default branch's head redetects the stack. The client gains branches()
and pullSnapshot().

* feat(sizing): add a DeepSeek fallback behind the Jira sizer

Sizing had one provider and one failure mode: an Anthropic key that was
missing, revoked, or out of credit raised `sizing_configuration`, which is
`stopsRun`, and the run stopped.

Add DeepSeekSizer, a thin adapter over DeepSeek's OpenAI-compatible
`/chat/completions`, and FallbackSizer to compose the two. Configured
together, DeepSeek answers whenever an Anthropic call fails — including the
`stopsRun` configuration case, which is precisely what an exhausted key looks
like. Configured alone, it serves sizing outright.

The adapter is `fetch` rather than a new SDK: the request is one forced tool
call, and the existing retry, deadline, and error-classification logic depends
on raw `status` and `retry-after` values that an SDK wrapper would normalize
away. It keeps the same injectable-client seam as AnthropicSizer, so the
same fake-driven tests extend to it. No new dependencies.

Two things had assumed the Anthropic pair specifically:

- The executor mounted on `sizingConfig`, so a DeepSeek-only deploy would
  have left the bounty routes unmounted. It now mounts on the sizer.
- `requestedModel` came from that pair and is `notNull` in the DB, with the
  routes refusing to start a run without it. It now comes from the sizer,
  which on a DeepSeek-only deploy is the only model there is.

`sizing_cancelled` never hands over: it means the run was aborted or its
deadline is spent, so a second provider would start against an already
aborted signal. When both fail, the fallback's error propagates, so the
`stopsRun` contract reflects the provider that had the last word.

DEEPSEEK_BASE_URL is env-only, not a secret — it is a proxy or gateway
address, so it is deliberately absent from secrets.tf and the push scripts.

* fix(sizing): make runs survive the DeepSeek fallback and close cleanly

A sizing run ended as "failed · 0 results" with `worker_lost` recorded,
which hid three separate faults stacked on top of each other.

Store: every lease-fenced update compared `lease_expires_at` and
`deadline_at` with a Date interpolated into a raw `sql` template. Drizzle's
postgres-js driver makes the timestamp serializers transparent, so the Date
reached the wire unmapped and the driver threw ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE. That
took out heartbeat, recordOutcome, finish, createForLease, and the writeback
claim and heartbeat: the executor threw before `finish`, and the watchdog
later relabelled the run `worker_lost`. Compare through the column with `gt`
instead. The store unit tests run on a fake that never serializes, so the
Postgres integration suite gains a case that drives all of these paths; it
fails on the old code.

DeepSeek: the current models run in thinking mode, and thinking mode rejects
a forced tool_choice with a 400 — which `isConfigurationError` turned into a
run stop, so the fallback failed exactly when it was needed. Sizing is one
bounded classification, so the request now turns thinking off.

Executor: the first fatal code aborts the controller, the other workers
report `sizing_cancelled`, and their `worker_lost` overwrote the cause. The
first code now wins. `bounty_executor_failed` also carries the thrown error
to the operator's log; it was a bare code before.

list below it, a bin on each row, and an "Add a board" button per site.

say which site a board is on without repeating it on every row. And
picking boards one at a time asked the person to repeat a decision they
had already made by connecting the site.

turning a real grant into a failed connection.

thing that matters: a sync refreshes only what is Jira's to state — the

subject: feat: remove the todo placeholder and add personal organizations (#37)
message:
* feat: remove the todo placeholder and give every user a personal organization

The todo domain was the scaffold this repository was initialised with. It is
gone: the table, the stores, the routes, the wire schemas, the web screen and
the core rules that described it. What outlived it moved rather than died —
`NotFoundError` now lives in `packages/db/src/errors.ts`, because the email,
organization and Jira routes all raise it for the same reason, and
`generateId` lost its `todo` default so every caller names its own prefix.

`packages/core` keeps the handle rules, which are a real domain rule: users
and organizations draw handles from one namespace, so what counts as valid has
to be decided once. `packages/client` and `apps/extension` stay as working
shells — `ApiClient` keeps the transport, auth and error contract, and the
extension keeps activation, its secret-backed token, Show Version and the
config-reload handler. Neither has a feature today; both are kept because the
editor surface is planned and rebuilding that wiring later is the cost avoided.

In its place, the ownership model the sandbox plan settled on
(docs/plan/2026-09-18-sandbox-context.md, decision 1) and then deferred:

Every user now gets a **personal organization** at signup — `kind = 'personal'`,
a sole `owner` member, handle equal to their username — created by the
`user.create.after` hook and backfilled for existing users by migration 0015.
This is what lets everything ownable take a single non-null `organization_id`
rather than a nullable user/organization pair, which would need a
`num_nonnulls(...) = 1` check drizzle-kit cannot generate and would double
every unique index and store path for the life of the schema.

A personal organization cannot gain members or be deleted: `refusePersonal` in
`auth.ts` guards the invitation, add-member and delete hooks, so "personal"
stays a claim about the organization rather than a label on a two-person one.
It goes when the user does, by the cascade on `personal_user_id`.

Nothing below the API boundary branches on `kind` — the membership is what
authorizes, whichever kind it is. Only surfaces distinguish them. `/` is now a
connections home listing every Jira site the person can reach, grouped by
owner with their personal organization first; `/o/:slug/jira` still shows one
organization's own. The organizations list labels and sorts the personal one
first, and its settings page hides members, invitations and leaving.

The backfill was verified against Postgres: handles already held by a team get
a numeric suffix, and a re-run inserts nothing.

* ci(cd): fail the deploy when ECS rolls it back

`aws ecs wait services-stable` succeeds on a *rolled-back* service: the
circuit breaker reverts to the previous task definition and the service is
then perfectly stable. So a deploy whose tasks could not start reported
success here and only failed five minutes later, in verify-deploy, with a
timeout that said nothing about why.

That is how production sat on the previous build while every run looked
almost-green. After the wait, compare the PRIMARY deployment's task definition
with the one this run registered; if they differ, say so, print the service
events that explain it, and point at the container's own logs — a rollback is
nearly always a missing secret or a failed migration, neither of which the
workflow log shows.

* fix(infra): treat the Jira credentials as optional in the secrets scripts

undefined, which leaves the Jira connect routes unmounted. But
`secrets-check.sh` checked them alongside the required providers, so an
otherwise-complete production config failed with "the API will not start",
which is untrue and sends you looking for a problem that is not there.

They are now their own check, with the rule that actually matters: both or
neither. One without the other reads as "Jira configured" to a human and as
"not configured" to the API, and only `jiraOAuthConfig` would ever say so.

`secrets-push.sh` refuses to write an empty value, which is right — a blank
would overwrite a live credential. Its message said every key is required at
boot, so the remedy it implied was to invent a value. It now says what the
two-pass write actually guarantees, and points at dropping an optional key
from `--only` instead.

Also dropped "the eight keys" from the missing-file help: there are eleven.

* fix(jira): strip trailing slashes without a backtracking regex

`siteUrl.replace(/\/+$/, "")` appeared in `ApiTokenCredential` and in
`toIssueDto`, both recovered verbatim from the lost package's compiled
output. CodeQL flagged both as high-severity ReDoS (alerts 72 and 73):

ending in many slashes takes O(n^2). Measured at ~1300ms for 60,000
slashes, which blocks the event loop for every other request the process
is serving.

`siteUrl` is not ours: it comes from Atlassian's accessible-resources
response and from the stored `jira_connection` row.

Replaced with a backwards scan in one shared helper, and pinned by a test
that fails on the old implementation (1300ms against a 250ms threshold)
while passing in 0ms on this one.

feat: deploy to AWS via CloudFront, Fargate and Neon (#32)
message:
* feat: deploy to AWS via CloudFront, Fargate and Neon

Serves platform.lunox.work from one CloudFront distribution: the SPA from a
private S3 bucket, /api/* from a Fargate task. One origin, because the app
already assumes one — apps/web/nginx.conf and the Vite dev proxy both put the
API under /api, so the session cookie stays host-only and no request needs a
CORS preflight.

Sized for the traffic it actually has (~$15/month) rather than the traffic it
might: no NAT Gateway ($32.85/mo), no load balancer ($16.43/mo), no RDS
($13.98/mo). ECS Service Discovery keeps a Route53 record pointed at the
running task, which is what an ALB would otherwise be paid to do, and Postgres
is Neon's free tier.

Dropping the load balancer removed the listener rule that enforced the
X-Origin-Verify header, so that check moves into the app: routes.ts gains
middleware, gated on an optional ORIGIN_VERIFY. Unset — locally, or behind a
load balancer — the check is not installed at all. /health is exempt so
container probes keep working.

CD runs on push to main, after the existing required checks have already
gated the merge. It migrates before rolling the service, publishes the SPA
after the API is stable, then asks /version whether the site is serving the
commit it just built — turning the repo's existing build-provenance machinery
into deploy verification.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(infra): point the origin record at the task's public IP

ECS Service Discovery cannot do the job it was given here. With awsvpc
networking it registers a task's *private* IP and offers no way to publish the
public one — correct for service-to-service traffic inside a VPC, and useless
to CloudFront, which resolves the origin from the public internet. The first
deploy produced a 502 from a task that was running, healthy, and answering
fine on its public address.

Replaced with an EventBridge rule and a small Python function: every ECS task
state change triggers a read of which tasks are RUNNING and an UPSERT of their
public IPs into api.platform.lunox.work. ~$0.20/month, against ~$16 for the
load balancer that is the sanctioned answer to the same problem.

The function's Route53 permission is scoped by three conditions — record name,
record type, and action — so a bug in it cannot touch the Zoho MX and DKIM
records that share the zone. It logs and skips rather than raising when no
task has a public IP: an exception would be retried, and retrying a stale
task-start event could publish an IP that has already been released.

Also drops the separate origin.lunox.work hosted zone, which existed only
because ECS owned every record in a namespace it managed. This function writes
one record by name, so that isolation no longer costs $0.50/month.

backend.hcl loses use_lockfile: that needs Terraform 1.10+ and this runs 1.5.7.
The alternative is a DynamoDB table, which is a resource to pay for so a single
operator cannot race themselves; CI only runs plan, which takes no lock.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* ci: let pull requests run terraform plan with a read-only role

The deploy role is scoped to `ref:refs/heads/main`, which is what stops a
fork's pull request from reaching AWS. It also means a pull request cannot run
`terraform plan` — the token carries `pull_request` in its `sub`, not a branch
ref — so every infrastructure PR failed the Plan job with "Not authorized to
perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity". Correct behaviour, useless signal: a
plan is most valuable on the PR that proposes the change.

Adds a second identity trusted for `repo:<this repo>:pull_request` and nothing
else, with ReadOnlyAccess attached. A fork's PR carries its own repository in
that claim, so it still cannot assume this role, and read-only means the worst
a compromised workflow can do here is look.

ReadOnlyAccess rather than an enumerated policy because `plan` refreshes every
resource in the state: a hand-written list would fail opaquely each time the
stack gains a resource type, and the property that matters is that nothing can
be mutated.

The workflow picks the role by trigger, so pushes to main keep using the
deploy role.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(infra): match GitHub's immutable OIDC subject claims

Both trust policies expected `repo:owner/name:...`, which never matches here:
this repository has GitHub's immutable subject claims enabled, so the `sub` in
an OIDC token is `repo:owner@<org id>/name@<repo id>:...`. The numeric ids pin
the claim to this exact repository even if it is renamed or transferred, which
is the point of the feature — and the reason the plain-name form silently fails
to match rather than erroring in some legible way.

Caught on the Plan job, which failed with "Not authorized to perform
sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity" against a role whose policy looked correct. The
deploy role carried the same mistake and would have failed the first CD run for
the same reason, several steps later and with more moving parts to rule out.

The prefix is a variable rather than assembled from var.github_repository,
because the ids are not derivable from the name — read them back with:

  gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/actions/oidc/customization/sub

* fix: address review findings from the deployment PR

Four real problems, found by CodeRabbit on #32.

**The deploy role could never have worked.** cd.yml declares
`environment: production`, and a job that does gets `:environment:<name>` in
its OIDC subject instead of the branch ref — so the trust policy, which only
listed the ref form, would have rejected every CD run. The policy now accepts
both, which does not widen it: each value still pins this repository and either
the main branch or the production environment.

**The task had no health check.** Without a load balancer nothing else asks the
API whether it can serve, so ECS would call a deployment stable because the
process was alive, stop the old task, and leave a running-but-broken one in
production. Adds the check the ALB's target group used to perform, via `node`
rather than curl or wget — the runtime image is node:22-alpine and ships
neither.

**A failing terraform plan could report success.** The step's shell is `bash -e`
without `pipefail`, so the pipeline returned tee's status and the job passed on
a plan that never completed.

**The deploy role's ECS permissions were account-wide.** Now split: the calls
that take no resource keep the wildcard AWS requires, and the ones that act on
a running service are pinned to this cluster.

* fix(infra): let the plan role read the secrets it plans

The pipefail fix in the previous commit did its job immediately: `terraform
plan` had been failing on the PR and reporting success, because the pipeline
returned tee's status. With that closed, the real error surfaced —

carries its own repository in the subject claim and is rejected.

* fix: address the second review pass

Four real problems from CodeRabbit's review of the rebased branch.

* fix: prune SPA assets by difference, not by age

The lifecycle rule added in the previous commit was a bad fix. It expired
everything under assets/ after 30 days, including the hashes the live
index.html points at — so a month without a deploy would have deleted the
running bundle, and the next CloudFront cache miss would have served an SPA
whose assets 404. Removed from the bucket as well as from the workflow.

Pruning by difference instead: delete what is in the bucket and not in the
directory just uploaded. The current set is never a candidate, however long
since the last deploy, and the old set goes immediately rather than after a
grace period — safe because index.html has already been flipped, so nothing
served from that point references it.

Also makes the origin-dns function honest about what it does not solve.
Read-then-write is not compare-and-swap: a stale invocation can still land
after a newer one. Proper serialisation needs a raised account quota plus
reserved concurrency, or a FIFO queue, and neither is done here. What is done
is a re-read immediately before publishing, so an invocation whose task died
mid-run drops out instead of writing a dead address — and a comment saying
plainly what residual risk remains and when to revisit it.

* fix: order origin-record writes by event time, and give asset pruning a grace period

Two follow-ups from review, both about the same class of mistake: treating a
window as closed when it was only narrowed.

**The origin record could still be restored to a dead IP.** A re-read before
publishing is not compare-and-swap, so an older invocation finishing late could
overwrite a newer one. Reserved concurrency is the obvious fix and is
unavailable: this account sits under the new-account Lambda limit of 10, below
which AWS refuses any reservation.

So the writes are ordered instead. Each carries the ECS event time it came
from, in a TXT record written in the same atomic Route53 change batch as the A
record, and an invocation stands down when it finds a marker from a newer
event. "Last writer wins" becomes "newest event wins". Verified against the
live record: a replayed 2020 event stands down with "superseded by a newer
event" while the record is broken, and the next current event repairs it.

**Pruning assets immediately broke already-open tabs.** Flipping index.html does
not retire the documents browsers are already holding, and one of those can
request a lazy-loaded chunk hours later. Pruning now requires an object to be
both absent from the current build and older than 24 hours, so the live set is
never a candidate and a stale tab has a day to finish.

* fix(ci): compare asset age numerically, not through a JMESPath filter

`Contents[?LastModified<='<string>']` relied on behaviour JMESPath does not
specify: its ordering operators are defined for numbers only, and a string
operand is specified to yield null, which drops every element. The result would
be a prune step that matches nothing, deletes nothing, and reports success —
invisible, and only noticed when the bucket had quietly grown for months.

This CLI build turns out to be more forgiving than the spec (a future cutoff
does return objects), so the step was working here. That is not worth depending
on across CLI versions when the failure mode is a silent no-op.

Converts both sides to epoch seconds in the shell and compares them there.

fix: trim handle hyphens without a backtracking regex (#21)
message:
CodeQL flagged `replace(/^-+|-+$/g, "")` in `toHandleBase` as a polynomial
ReDoS. On a local part that is a long run of hyphens, the `-+$` alternative
retries from every offset before failing, which is quadratic in the length
of the run.

The input is the local part of a provider-supplied address, so it is not
ours to bound, and the truncation to USERNAME_MAX_LENGTH happens after the
trim rather than before, so it does not cap the work either.

Index arithmetic has no such failure mode. Verified identical to the regex
across the edge cases and several thousand fuzzed inputs, including the
all-hyphen string that trims to empty.

subject: feat(bounties): select tickets by category and browse proposals by category (#64)
message:
* feat(bounties): size every ticket that fits a category, with the reason

A backlog run took the ten oldest tickets. It now reads the whole board and
sizes every open ticket that fits at least one outsourcing category, and
records why each was picked.

Categories are one registry in packages/core/src/selection: Left behind,
Always next sprint, Quietly wanted, Holding others up, Paper cuts and
Deadline exposed. Each is an id, a label, default thresholds and a rule
built from named signals, so a criterion or a category changes in one
place. The board settings schema is generated from the registry, and a
board can override any threshold or switch a category off.

- Selection reads /board/{id}/issue for every board type, asking for
  sprint history, votes, watchers, links and fix versions, and classifies
  in code. The backlog endpoint hides tickets in a sprint, which are what
  "Always next sprint" looks for. Still no description in a list read.
- The reason is stored on the run's plan and shown on proposal rows, in
  the sizing list, and in the peek under "Why this ticket".
- maxTickets and excludeAssigned become ticketCap (optional, no default)
  and unassignedOnly (default false). Renamed rather than re-defaulted:
  registration stored the old defaults on existing boards, which would
  have kept them capped at ten.
- A run's deadline grows with its plan, and recorded outcomes are bounded
  by the plan rather than a fixed 50.
- Board settings merge category by category and threshold by threshold,
  and a null in an update removes the setting instead of being stored.
- The proposal list pages 50 at a time with "Show more", and title
  streams are split into batches the route accepts.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(bounties): browse proposals by category, with an icon for each

A run now sizes every ticket that fits a category, so a board's proposal
list is long and mixed. The board page gains a view over it: a row of tiles
above the table, one per category with its count, that narrows the list to
the tickets picked for that reason.

- Tiles are All, the six categories in registry order, then Uncategorized
  for proposals with no category recorded (picked by hand, or sized before
  there were categories). A category with nothing in it is shown dimmed and
  cannot be pressed, so the tiles are always the same ones. The choice is
  in the URL as ?category=, beside ?proposal=.
- Counts and filtering happen in the database, because the list is paged:
  GET /jira/boards/:id/proposal-categories returns the counts with each
  category's label and why-text from the registry, and ?category= on
  GET /proposals filters. Both read the category from the run's plan. A
  malformed id is a 400; an id no category has is an empty list.
- A re-price moved the proposal onto a run whose plan had no categories,
  so "Re-analyze" dropped a ticket out of its category. The executor now
  copies the categories from the plan the proposal came from.
- A row under a chosen category leads with that category's reason, and the
  reason wraps on a phone instead of being cut off.
- Each category has its own drawn icon, on Lucide's grid, shown on its
  tile, on the row's reason line and in the peek. The drawings live in the
  web app, keyed by category id; an id without one falls back to a tag
  icon, and a test walks the registry so a new category cannot ship
  without its drawing.
